points: Couples now tend to marry later, often after completing their education and establishing a career.
Cohabitation, living together without being married, has become common and is widely accepted.
Marriage is no longer seen as the only acceptable basis for a family, and many children are born to parents who are not married.
Divorce became legal in Ireland after a referendum in 1995, and the Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996 sets out the conditions for granting one.

Under that Act, a divorce may be granted only where the spouses have lived apart for four of the previous five years, there is no reasonable prospect of reconciliation, and proper provision has been made for the spouse and dependants.
Judicial separation, provided for under the Judicial Separation and Family Law Reform Act 1989, allows spouses to live apart under a court order that deals with maintenance and property.
The 2015 marriage referendum allowed same-sex couples to marry, reflecting wider acceptance of different types of family.
Parenting has become more child-centred, with greater emphasis on children's views, open communication and negotiated rules.
Physical punishment of children by parents is prohibited by Irish law.
Smaller families are now more common, as contraception lets couples plan the number and timing of their children.
Mothers and fathers increasingly share childcare, and paternity leave recognises the role of the father.
Parental leave allows parents to take unpaid time off work to care for children.
Grandparents often take on regular childcare, particularly where both parents work outside the home.
Traditional roles assigned the male as breadwinner and the female as homemaker, with responsibilities kept largely separate.
Egalitarian roles, where partners share finances, housework, discipline and decisions, are now more common.
A man taking on the role of house husband or primary carer is now socially accepted.
The decline in the influence of the Church lessened expectations about marriage, sexuality and parental roles.
Children may take on more responsibility for household tasks, and older children may look after younger siblings.
Family diversity means that nuclear, extended, lone-parent, blended, cohabiting and same-sex-parent families are all recognised as families.
Improved education, particularly for women, has widened choices about careers, marriage and having children.
Contraception and family planning allowed couples to plan families and delay childbearing.
Urbanisation and greater mobility loosened the influence of extended family and the local community.
Greater personal freedom and individual choice came to be valued over duty to family or community.
Media and international influences introduced new ideas about relationships and family life.

keyTerms.definition: Living together as a couple without being legally married.
A pattern of family roles in which partners share responsibilities such as finances, housework and childcare equally.
A division of responsibilities in which the father earns the income and the mother runs the home and cares for children.
A court order allowing spouses to live apart, dealing with maintenance and property, without ending the marriage.
A family in which one parent lives with and cares for one or more children.
A family formed when a parent with children marries or cohabits with a partner who may also have children.
An approach to raising children that gives weight to their views, needs and participation in decisions.
A family made up of two parents and their children living together.
Methods used to prevent pregnancy, allowing couples to plan the number and timing of children.

factCards.term: Three conditions for granting a divorce under Irish law
factCards.definition: The spouses have lived apart for four of the previous five years, there is no reasonable prospect of reconciliation, and proper provision has been made for the spouse and dependants.

factCards.term: Three shifts in attitudes to parenting
factCards.definition: More child-centred decision-making, shared childcare between mothers and fathers, and smaller family size.

factCards.term: Four causes of changing attitudes to family life
factCards.definition: Better education for women, contraception, urbanisation and mobility, and personal freedom.

factCards.term: Four types of modern family structure
factCards.definition: Nuclear, extended, lone-parent and blended families.

questions.prompt: Name two changes in attitudes to marriage in Ireland in recent decades.
questions.model: Couples marry later, often after completing education and establishing a career. Cohabitation without marriage is widely accepted. Many children are born to parents who are not married. Divorce is available under the Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996.

questions.prompt: Explain how attitudes to parenting and to traditional family roles have changed, and describe the effects of these changes on children.
questions.model: Parenting has become more child-centred, with children's views and negotiated rules given weight, and physical punishment is prohibited by law. Smaller families, made possible by contraception, mean parents can give each child more attention. Traditional roles of male breadwinner and female homemaker have given way to egalitarian sharing of finances, housework, discipline and childcare, and fathers can take paternity leave. Children may gain more say in family decisions and may take on more household responsibility, or look after younger siblings. Where both parents work, children may rely more on grandparents or childcare services, and may experience less time with their parents.
